title: Learning When to Think: Adaptive Test-Time Compute
hook: Let the model pick its own thinking budget with its very first token. On MATH500 that cut response length 41% while accuracy barely moved.
key_points: Fixed reasoning budgets over-compute on easy problems and under-compute on hard ones.
The model emits one of three modes as its first token: NoThink, Short, or Long — no separate router model.
Mode choice is learned inside GRPO via a shaped reward that makes each mode pay off at a different response length, plus hard per-mode token caps.
On a 1.5B distilled model trained on MATH, all three modes survive rather than collapsing to one.
MATH500 over three seeds: 0.782 vs 0.796 baseline accuracy, mean length 2,811 vs 4,796 tokens (41% less).
It transfers without retraining — 76% token reduction on the easier GSM8K, at higher accuracy than baselines of similar length.
content_html: Reasoning models trained with RL usually think for a fixed token budget, which is wrong in both directions: wasted compute on easy problems, not enough on hard ones. Kassenaar, Yang, and François-Lavet ask whether a model can learn to allocate its own effort, and give it a very direct interface — the first token of the response selects a mode: NoThink (answer immediately), Short (brief reasoning), or Long (extended reasoning).
extra_html:
How it's trained

The choice is learned inside Group Relative Policy Optimization, with no separate router. Two ingredients keep it from degenerating: a shaped reward that makes each mode the best option at a different response length, and hard per-mode token caps that stop the modes blurring together. Trained on MATH with a 1.5B distilled model, all three modes persist. The authors read a useful signal out of this — the brief modes end up more accurate than Long, which means the policy is sorting problems by difficulty rather than choosing at random.

Results

Averaged over three seeds on held-out MATH500, accuracy stays close to the base model (0.782 vs 0.796) while mean response length drops from 4,796 to 2,811 tokens, a 41% reduction. The policy also transfers to other benchmarks without retraining, saving most where problems are easiest: 76% fewer tokens on GSM8K, at higher accuracy than baselines constrained to similar lengths.

related.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute
related.hook: A new scaling axis: instead of a bigger model, let a model think longer at inference — often a better use of compute, and the principle behind o1 and R1.

related.title: When More Sampling Hurts: The Modal Ceiling and Correlation Ceiling of Test-Time Scaling
related.hook: Sample a reasoning model dozens of times and coverage keeps climbing — but picking the right answer from the pile plateaus fast, and extra samples past that point can backfire.

related.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
related.hook: DeepSeek shows strong reasoning can emerge from RL on verifiable rewards with minimal supervised data - and those reasoning traces can be distilled into smaller models.

flashcards.prompt: How does the model express its reasoning-budget decision?
flashcards.back_html: As the first token of its response — NoThink, Short, or Long — so the routing decision is part of the policy itself rather than a separate router.

flashcards.prompt: What evidence shows the learned mode choice tracks difficulty rather than firing at random?

choices.text: The brief modes end up more accurate than Long, meaning easy problems were sorted into them
All three modes are chosen with equal frequency
Long mode achieves the highest accuracy of the three

flashcards.explanation_html: If routing were random, per-mode accuracy would be similar. Short/NoThink scoring higher than Long implies the policy is sending genuinely easier problems to the cheap modes.

flashcards.prompt: What keeps the three modes from collapsing into one during GRPO training?
flashcards.back_html: A shaped reward that makes each mode worthwhile at a different response length, combined with hard per-mode token caps that keep them behaviorally distinct.
